I have been farming this wheat-maize rotation in Quzhou for twenty years, and I know what works on my 10.1 mu of land. My family has four people, and with some of us working off-farm, I do not have extra labor to waste. I have a well, so I can irrigate when the rain does not come, but I still watch every cost.

For my **winter wheat**, I will plant an improved variety like Shimai or Lumai. These seeds are reliable, and I know how they behave on my land. Before sowing in October, I will rotary till the field to break up the stubble and prepare a good seedbed. I will put down about 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu as a basal dose — that gives me roughly 18 kg of nitrogen, 11 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium per mu in total nutrients. Then, when the wheat greens up in spring and reaches jointing, I will top-dress with urea. I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings establish, once at jointing, and once during grain filling. I will spray four times for weeds, rust, and aphids. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 500 kg per mu.

For **summer maize**, timing is everything — I only have a few days after wheat harvest in early June to get the seed in the ground before the season slips away. So I will not till; I will sow directly into the wheat stubble. I will use a hybrid variety like Denghai 605 or Nongda 372. Hybrid seed costs more, but the yield gain pays for itself. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing — about 80 jin per mu — which gives me roughly 11 kg nitrogen, 3 kg phosphorus, and 3 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate twice in summer if the rains are thin, and I will spray pesticides three times for weeds, corn borers, and leaf diseases. I expect around 550 kg per mu from the maize.

I keep my fertilizer and irrigation at these levels because that is what my neighbors do, what the seed shop recommends, and what has given me stable yields year after year. I do not chase record yields — I chase reliable income.
